newsitem.title: SPAIN: SOCCER-SPANISH PLAYERS UNION MOVES TO STEM 'FOREIGN INVASION'.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SPANISH PLAYERS UNION MOVES TO STEM 'FOREIGN INVASION'.

text.p: Spanish soccer players, angry that foreigners are threatening their careers, decided in a union meeting on Monday to take their case to the country's sporting authorities.
"We want to redress a situation that seems alarming. We've got 200 foreigners playing here," said Gerardo Movilla, president of the Association of Spanish Footballers.
A delegation from the association will discuss the matter with the Supreme Council of Sport, the clubs and the Spanish Federation.
The meeting was held in the wake of the Bosman decision which lifted restrictions on the number of foriegners playing in overseas teams.

While the Spaniards can do nothing about changing the rules as they now relate following the Bosman decision, they could do something about the legislation allowing Latin Americans to acquire Spanish nationality after just two years' residence further reduces the opportunities available to home-grown talent.
The situation has been accentuated by lucrative new television contracts which have financed the influx of foreign stars.
The association would like to see a gradual reduction in the number of non-EU players allowed per team.
Movilla is reluctant to talk of a strike, but that is a definite possibility after the players successfully used the threat of a Christmas boycott to change the league calendar.
A number of commentators are concerned that the national side will suffer as a result of what the country's press calls 'the foreign invasion'.
The Spanish basketball team has slumped noticeably since the country's league increased the number of foreigners allowed on court from two to three per team.
"We're doing it for the good of the Spanish game, and because our players have got as much, or more quality as the foreigners," said Movilla.
His opinion has been echoed by a number of players who feel slighted by the arrival of so much international talent.

"Not all the foreigners give as much quality as Spaniards who aren't playing," said Atletico Madrid's Carlos Aguilera who would normally have expected to find a space in the Spanish champions' team but has been kept out by the presence of eight foreign-born players.
"The Spanish player has got to be protected, and a limit placed on the number of foreigners," said Valencia defender Jorge Otero.
The issue is to be discussed again in March once the delegations have made contact with the sports authorities and clubs.
